Take-Home Exercise 1

Author

Serene Cheng

Published

May 22, 2026

Modified

May 24, 2026

Introduction

Background

Insurers often manage portfolios whereby the cause of poor profitability and high volatility are not immediately clear. These outcomes may be influenced by a combination of customer profiles, policy, characteristics, claim patterns and it changes over time. This study uses a real-world open-access motor vehicle insurance portfolio dataset and visual analytics libraries in R to explore numerical, categorical, and temporal variables, with the aim of identifying key factors influencing portfolio profitability and volatility.

The Data

This study uses a real-world motor vehicle insurance portfolio dataset obtained from a Spanish insurance company that specialises in non-life insurance. The dataset, together with its accompanying cookbook, is publicly available through Mendeley Data.

Objectives

The objectives of this study are:

  • To apply suitable univariate visual analytics techniques to explore the distributions and characteristics of key numerical and categorical variables in the insurance portfolio dataset.
  • To apply suitable bivariate visual analytics techniques to investigate relationships between variables and statistically validate factors influencing the profitability and volatility of the insurance portfolio.

Getting started

Loading packages

Begin by loading the following R packages using the p_load() function in the pacman package.

Package Description
tidyverse Collection of R packages commonly used for data importing, wrangling, transformation and visualisation. Includes ggplot2, dplyr, tidyr and other core packages.
ggdist Used to create distribution-based charts such as half-eye plots, which help show spread, skewness and central tendency
ggridges Creates ridgeline plots to compare numerical distributions across categories
patchwork Used to combine multiple ggplot charts into one composite figure, such as placing a boxplot above a histogram
scales Used to format chart labels, such as adding commas to large numbers or displaying percentages
corrplot Used to create correlation matrix visualisations
rstatix Used to run statistical validation tests such as correlation tests, Kruskal-Wallis tests, Wilcoxon tests and chi-square tests
gganimate Used to create animated ggplot visualisations, allowing temporal trends to be displayed as frame-by-frame animations
gifski Used to render animations as GIF files, working in conjunction with gganimate to produce animated graphics 
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, ggdist, ggridges, patchwork, scales, corrplot, rstatix, gganimate, gifski)

Data importing

The motor insurance portfolio data is imported into R using read_delim() function of readr package. read_delim() is used because the data file is semi-colon separated

motor_insurance <- read_delim("data/Dataset of motor insurance portfolio.csv", delim = ";", show_col_types = FALSE)

Data Wrangling

1. Check for duplicates

No record found for duplicated rows

sum(duplicated(motor_insurance))
[1] 0

No records found for duplicated policy-year records.

motor_insurance %>%
  count(insured_id, year) %>%
  filter(n > 1)
# A tibble: 0 × 3
# ℹ 3 variables: insured_id <dbl>, year <dbl>, n <int>

2. Check for missing values by column

motor_insurance %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "missing_count"
  ) %>%
  filter(missing_count > 0) %>%
  arrange(desc(missing_count))
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  variable            missing_count
  <chr>                       <int>
1 fuel_type                    1287
2 vehicle_value                 513
3 vehicle_age                     2
4 age_driving_licence             2

The largest missing column is fuel_type with 1,287 missing rows followed by vehicle_value, vehicle_age and age_driving_licence. We will first do variable selection then drop the rows with missing values.

3. Variable Selection

The original dataset contains 42 columns covering policy details, driver and vehicle characteristics, premium components, claim counts, incurred losses, and exposure. To keep the visual analysis focused, only variables that are relevant to overall portfolio profitability, volatility and potential loss drivers are retained.

Detailed coverage-level premium, claim, and incurred loss variables were excluded from the main analysis because the focus is on overall portfolio-level profitability and volatility.

Variables Retain Reason
year Retained as temporal variable to examine changes across years
policy_status To compare active and cancelled policies
policy_type Different coverage may have different premium and claim behavior
business_type To compare new and existing portfolio policies
bonus_score Reflect policyholder’s past claims experience and may influence future claim risk
driver_age Key driver characteristics that may affect claim frequency and risk behavior
vehicle_age Older vehicle may have different claim patterns, repair needs or loss severity
age_driving_licence Kept to derive driving_experience which is more meaningful for analysis
fuel_type To explore whether diesel and gasoline vehicles show different claim/profitability patterns
vehicle_value Vehicle value can influence claim severity and potential incurred losses
vehicle_brand For segment-level analysis, compare top vehicle brands by loss ratio or claim frequency
circulation_area To compare urban and rural driving environments which may influence claim exposure and frequency
municipality_type Retained as geographic indicator to examine whether different areas diff in risk and profitability
total_premium For measuring revenue and deriving loss ratio and underwriting profit
total_claims For measuring claim frequency and portfolio volatility
total_incurred For measuring total claim cost and portfolio volatility
total_exposure For normalising claims by time-on-risk to allow fair comparison across policies 
motor_insurance_selected <- motor_insurance %>%
  select(
    year,
    policy_status,
    policy_type,
    business_type,
    bonus_score,
    driver_age,
    vehicle_age,
    age_driving_licence,
    fuel_type,
    vehicle_value,
    vehicle_brand,
    circulation_area,
    municipality_type,
    total_premium,
    total_claims,
    total_incurred,
    total_exposure
  )

4. Dropping rows with missing value

Since the overall number of affected rows is small relative to the dataset size, rows with missing values were removed for completeness before visual analysis.

motor_insurance_clean <- motor_insurance_selected %>%
  drop_na()
nrow(motor_insurance) - nrow(motor_insurance_clean)
[1] 1802

After applying drop_na(), a total of 1,802 rows were removed. 1,802 / 354,140 = 0.51% which is considered as not significant

5. Variable Transformation

i. Creating a new variable from existing variables

After variable selection, new analytical variables were derived to investigate the portfolio’s profitability and volatility. driving_experience was created by subtracting age_driving_licence from driver_age to approximate the number of years the driver has held a licence.

Several profitability-related measures were also derived including: - loss_ratio (total_incurred/total_premium): Measures claims incurred relative to premium collected. Used as a profitability indicator - underwriting_profit (total_premium - total_incurred): Measures simplified underwriting profit before expenses, commissions, reinsurance, and investment income - claim_frequency (total_claims/total_exposure): Measures how often claims occur after adjusting for time-on-risk. Used to assess claim activity and volatility - claim_severity (total_incurred/total_claims): Measures the average incurred cost per claim. Used to assess the size or severity of claims.

These variables are created in accordance with actuarial/industry standards

motor_insurance_final <- motor_insurance_clean %>%
  mutate(
    driving_experience = driver_age - age_driving_licence,
    loss_ratio = total_incurred / total_premium,
    claim_frequency = total_claims / total_exposure,
    claim_severity = if_else(total_claims > 0, total_incurred / total_claims, NA_real_),
    underwriting_profit = total_premium - total_incurred
  ) %>%
  select(-age_driving_licence)

ii. Changing data type

After deriving the new variables, the data types were reviewed to ensure that each variable is treated appropriately for visual analysis. Variables such as policy_status, policy_type, business_type, bonus_score, fuel_type, vehicle_brand, circulation_area, and municipality_type were converted from character variables into factors because they represent categorical groups rather than continuous values.

Numerical variables such as driver_age, vehicle_age, vehicle_value, total_premium, total_claims, total_incurred, total_exposure, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, claim_severity, and underwriting_profit were kept as numeric variables for distribution analysis, correlation analysis, and bivariate visualisation.

motor_insurance_final <- motor_insurance_final %>%
  mutate(
    policy_status = as.factor(policy_status),
    policy_type = as.factor(policy_type),
    business_type = as.factor(business_type),
    bonus_score = as.factor(bonus_score),
    fuel_type = as.factor(fuel_type),
    vehicle_brand = as.factor(vehicle_brand),
    circulation_area = as.factor(circulation_area),
    municipality_type = as.factor(municipality_type)
  )

iii. Recoding categorical variables

Some categorical variables were originally coded using short labels. These were recoded into more descriptive labels to improve the readability of the visualisations.

motor_insurance_final <- motor_insurance_final %>%
  mutate(
    policy_status = recode(policy_status,
                           "A" = "Active",
                           "C" = "Cancelled"),
    business_type = recode(business_type,
                           "NB" = "New Business",
                           "P" = "Portfolio"),
    bonus_score = recode(bonus_score,
                         "G" = "Good",
                         "N" = "Neutral",
                         "B" = "Bad"),
    fuel_type = recode(fuel_type,
                       "D" = "Diesel",
                       "G" = "Gasoline"),
    circulation_area = recode(circulation_area,
                              "U" = "Urban",
                              "R" = "Rural"),
    municipality_type = recode(municipality_type,
                               "I" = "Inland",
                               "C" = "Coastal",
                               "IS" = "Islands")
  )

6. Final Variables Selected for Visual Analysis

Analysis Area Variables Used
Policy/Policyholder profile year, policy_status, policy_type, business_type, bonus_score, driver_age, age_driving_licence
Vehicle profile vehicle_age, fuel_type, vehicle_value, vehicle_brand
Geographic / driving environment circulation_area, municipality_type
Premium and exposure total_premium, total_exposure
Claims and incurred losses total_claims, total_incurred
Derived profitability variables loss_ratio, underwriting_profit
Derived volatility variables claim_frequency, claim_severity
Derived driver variable driving_experience

Univariate Visual Analytics

Not all retained variables were visualised individually in the univariate analysis. Some variables were retained because they were required to derive analytical measures such as loss_ratio, `claim_frequency, claim_severity, and underwriting_profit, while others were kept as supporting variables for bivariate analysis. The univariate analysis focuses on variables most relevant to portfolio composition, driver and vehicle profile, profitability, and claim volatility

1. Policy/Policyholder profile

1.1 Policy Type

  • Plot
  • Code
# Main count table
policy_type_summary <- motor_insurance_final %>%
  count(policy_type) %>%
  mutate(
    percentage = n / sum(n) * 100,
    label = paste0(scales::comma(n), "\n(", round(percentage, 1), "%)")
  )

# Reorder factor levels for plotting
policy_type_summary <- policy_type_summary %>%
  mutate(
    policy_type = factor(
      policy_type,
      levels = c("TP", "COMP_N", "TPG", "COMP_E", "CC")
    )
  )

# Description table for annotation on the right
policy_desc <- tibble(
  policy_type = factor(
    c("CC", "COMP_E", "TPG", "COMP_N", "TP"),
    levels = levels(policy_type_summary$policy_type)
  ),
  desc = c(
    "CC: Third-party liability with two or more additional coverages",
    "COMP_E: Comprehensive with excess",
    "TPG: Third-party liability with glass coverage",
    "COMP_N: Comprehensive without excess",
    "TP: Basic third-party liability only"
  ),
  xpos = c(260000, 260000, 260000, 260000, 260000)
)

ggplot(policy_type_summary, aes(x = policy_type, y = n, fill = policy_type)) +
  geom_col(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = label),
    hjust = -0.1,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = policy_desc,
    aes(x = policy_type, y = xpos, label = desc),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    hjust = 0,
    size = 3.2,
    colour = "black"
  ) +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::comma,
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.55))
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Policy Type",
    subtitle = "Shows the coverage mix of the insurance portfolio",
    x = "Policy Type",
    y = "Number of Policies"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 180, b = 10, l = 10)
  )
NoteInsights

  • The portfolio is dominated by CC policies. CC accounts for 204,317 policies (58.0%) of the portfolio.

  • Most policies include third-party liability with two or more additional coverages.

  • COMP_E is the second largest group with 90,320 policies (25.6%).

  • TPG accounts for 35,988 policies (10.2%).

  • COMP_N and TP make up much smaller shares at 4.5% and 1.6% respectively.

  • Overall, portfolio is more concentrated in broader coverage types rather than basic third-party-only policies.

1.2 Bonus Score

  • Plot
  • Code
motor_insurance_final %>%
  filter(!is.na(bonus_score)) %>%
  count(bonus_score) %>%
  mutate(
    percentage = n / sum(n) * 100,
    bonus_score = factor(
      bonus_score,
      levels = c("Good", "Neutral", "Bad")
    ),
    label = paste0(scales::comma(n), "\n(", round(percentage, 1), "%)")
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = bonus_score, y = n, fill = bonus_score)) +
  geom_col(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = label),
    vjust = -0.4,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::comma,
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.25))
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Pastel1") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Bonus Score",
    subtitle = "Shows the past claims profile of policyholders",
    x = "Bonus Score",
    y = "Number of Policies"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.margin = margin(t = 20, r = 10, b = 10, l = 10)
  )
NoteInsights
  • The portfolio is heavily dominated by policyholders with a Good bonus score.
  • Good bonus score accounts for 339,836 policies (96.5%).
  • This suggests that most policyholders have a favourable past claims history.
  • Neutral and Bad bonus score accounts for 7,809 policies (2.2%) and 4,693 policies (1.3%) respectively
  • Although the Neutral and Bad groups are small, they can still be explored further in bivariate analysis to see whether they are linked to higher claim_frequency or poorer loss_ratio.

1.3 Driver Age

  • Plot
  • Code
# Summary statistics
mean_age <- round(mean(motor_insurance_final$driver_age, na.rm = TRUE), 0)
median_age <- round(median(motor_insurance_final$driver_age, na.rm = TRUE), 0)
sd_age <- round(sd(motor_insurance_final$driver_age, na.rm = TRUE), 1)

# Boxplot
driver_age_box <- ggplot(motor_insurance_final, aes(x = driver_age, y = "")) +
  geom_boxplot(
    fill = "grey80",
    colour = "grey30",
    outlier.colour = "grey50",
    outlier.alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "point",
    colour = "coral",
    size = 3
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(20, 85, by = 5)
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(20, 85)) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Driver Age",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )

# Histogram
driver_age_hist <- ggplot(motor_insurance_final, aes(x = driver_age)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 20,
    fill = "steelblue",
    colour = "white"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = mean_age,
    colour = "coral",
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = median_age,
    colour = "blue",
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = median_age - 6,
    y = 39500,
    label = paste0("Median = ", median_age),
    colour = "blue",
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = mean_age + 6,
    y = 43000,
    label = paste0("Mean = ", mean_age),
    colour = "coral",
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 72,
    y = 43000,
    label = paste0("SD = ", sd_age),
    colour = "grey30",
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(20, 85, by = 5)
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(20, 85)) +
  labs(
    x = "Driver Age",
    y = "Number of Policies"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Combine boxplot and histogram
driver_age_box / driver_age_hist +
  plot_layout(heights = c(1, 3))
NoteInsights

  • Most insured drivers are concentrated between 35 and 65 years old, with the highest number of policies around the 40 to 45 age range.

  • This suggests that the portfolio is mainly made up of middle-aged drivers, while very young and very old drivers form a smaller share.

  • The distribution is slightly right-skewed, with policy counts gradually declining as driver age increases beyond the mid-40s.

2. Vehicle Profile

2.1 Vehicle Value

We can see from the initial boxplot distribution that vehicle value is highly right-skewed, with most insured vehicles concentrated at lower values and a small number of very high-value vehicles appearing as outliers. This suggests that the portfolio mainly consists of lower to mid-value vehicles, while a smaller group of luxury or high-value vehicles may have greater potential claim severity.

  • Plot
  • Code
# Summary statistics
mean_vehicle_value <- round(mean(motor_insurance_final$vehicle_value, na.rm = TRUE), 0)
median_vehicle_value <- round(median(motor_insurance_final$vehicle_value, na.rm = TRUE), 0)
sd_vehicle_value <- round(sd(motor_insurance_final$vehicle_value, na.rm = TRUE), 0)

# Boxplot
vehicle_value_box <- ggplot(motor_insurance_final, aes(x = vehicle_value, y = "")) +
  geom_boxplot(
    fill = "grey80",
    colour = "grey30",
    outlier.colour = "grey50",
    outlier.alpha = 0.35
  ) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "point",
    colour = "black",
    size = 3
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100000)) +

2.3 Vehicle Brand

Vehicle brand is visualised using a bar chart of the top 10 brands by policy count. Since there may be many vehicle brands, only the most common brands are shown individually, while the remaining brands are grouped under Others to keep the chart readable.

# Identify top 10 vehicle brands by policy count
top_vehicle_brands <- motor_insurance_final %>%

  filter(!is.na(vehicle_brand)) %>%

      as.character(vehicle_brand),
      "Others"
    )

  count(vehicle_brand_grouped, name = "n") %>%
  mutate(
    percentage = n / sum(n),

  )

4. Derived profitability variables

4.1 Loss Ratio and Loss Ratio Group

The histogram shows that loss_ratio is highly concentrated near zero, mainly because many policies have no incurred claims. There are also a small number of extreme high loss ratio values, where incurred claims are much larger than premiums. This makes the raw numerical distribution difficult to interpret using a standard histogram.

loss_ratio_data <- motor_insurance_final %>%
  filter(is.finite(loss_ratio))

ggplot(loss_ratio_data, aes(x = loss_ratio)) +
  geom_histogram(

    x = "Loss Ratio",

Data transformation is performed to change loss ratio into categorical variable

motor_insurance_final <- motor_insurance_final %>%
  mutate(
    loss_ratio_group = case_when(
      loss_ratio == 0 ~ "No Loss",
      loss_ratio > 0 & loss_ratio <= 1 ~ "Profitable / Acceptable",
      loss_ratio > 1 ~ "Loss-making"
    )
  )

      loss_ratio_group,

  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = loss_ratio_group, y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "mediumpurple", colour = "white") +

    subtitle = "Loss ratio was grouped to improve interpretability of the profitability profile",
    x = "Loss Ratio Group",
    y = "Number of Policies"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.margin = margin(t = 20, r = 10, b = 10, l = 10)
  )
NoteInsights

  • Most policies fall under the No Loss group, meaning they did not record any incurred claims during the exposure period.

  • This is expected in insurance portfolios, where many policyholders do not make claims within a given year.

  • A smaller proportion falls under Profitable / Acceptable, where incurred claims are positive but do not exceed premium collected.

  • The Loss-making group is smaller but important, as these policies have incurred claims greater than premium and may drive profitability pressure in the portfolio.

Spearman Correlation

  • Plot
  • Code
# Select numerical variables for Spearman correlation
spearman_data <- motor_insurance_final %>%
  select(
    driver_age,
    vehicle_age,
    driving_experience,
    vehicle_value,
    total_premium,
    total_incurred,
    total_claims,
    loss_ratio,
    claim_frequency,
    claim_severity,
    underwriting_profit
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    across(everything(), ~ ifelse(is.finite(.), ., NA))
  )

# Compute Spearman correlation matrix
spearman_cor_matrix <- cor(
  spearman_data,
  use = "pairwise.complete.obs",
  method = "spearman"
)

# Plot Spearman correlation matrix
corrplot::corrplot(
  spearman_cor_matrix,
  method = "color",
  type = "upper",
  order = "hclust",
  addCoef.col = "black",
  number.cex = 0.65,
  tl.col = "black",
  tl.srt = 45,
  tl.cex = 0.8,
  col = colorRampPalette(c("#4D96FF", "white", "#FF6B6B"))(200),
  title = "Spearman Correlation Matrix of Numerical Variables",
  mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0)
)
NoteFindings

  • Spearman correlation results show that most numerical variables have weak or near-zero relationships with the key insurance outcomes, suggesting that no single variable strongly explains claim frequency, claim severity or loss ratio on its own.

  • Age-related variables such as driver_age, vehicle_age and driving_experience show very low correlations with the outcome variables. This suggests that age may not have a strong direct monotonic relationship with profitability or claims outcomes in this dataset.

  • Stronger patterns are likely to be found through categorical group comparisons or segmented analysis instead of correlation alone, since insurance risk may depend on non-linear effects, policy type, bonus score, vehicle characteristics or claim history.

A separate correlation matrix was also considered for claim policies only, since claim severity is more meaningful when a claim has occurred. This helps reduce the effect of zero-claim policies and provides a clearer view of relationships among claim-related variables.

NoteFindings
  • After filtering to policies with claims only, the claim-related variables show stronger relationships. total_incurred has a strong positive correlation with claim_severity (0.91), which makes sense because severity increases when the incurred claim amount is higher.
  • total_claims and claim_frequency also show a strong positive correlation (0.70), suggesting that policies with more claims naturally tend to have higher claim frequency.
  • Age-related variables such as driver_age, vehicle_age and driving_experience still show near-zero correlations with claim outcomes, suggesting that age-related factors may not have a strong monotonic relationship with claim severity, frequency or loss ratio in this dataset.

Bivariate Visual Analysis

The Spearman correlation analysis showed that most numerical variables had weak or near-zero monotonic relationships with the key insurance outcomes, such as claim frequency, claim severity, loss ratio and underwriting profit. This suggests that the relationships in the dataset may not be strongly linear or direct.

Therefore, the bivariate visual analysis focuses on selected variables that are more meaningful from an insurance and business perspective, such as policy type, bonus score, vehicle characteristics and age-related groups. Instead of using every variable, selected charts are used to check whether clearer patterns appear through categorical group comparisons, segmented distributions or non-linear relationships. This helps keep the analysis focused while also avoiding repetitive charts where the correlation results already suggest limited direct relationship.

Profitability

1. Loss Ratio Group vs Policy Type

The stacked percentage bar chart is used to compare the relationship between two categorical variables: policy_type and loss_ratio_group. The x-axis represents the different policy types, while the y-axis shows the percentage of policies within each policy type. Each bar is divided into three profitability groups: No Loss, Profitable / Acceptable, and Loss-making. Using percentages instead of raw counts allows the profitability composition of each policy type to be compared fairly, even though some policy types have many more policies than others. This visualisation helps identify whether certain policy types have a higher proportion of loss-making policies, which may indicate poorer profitability performance.

  • Plot
  • Code
profitability_policy <- motor_insurance_final %>%
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio_group), !is.na(policy_type)) %>%
  count(policy_type, loss_ratio_group) %>%
  group_by(policy_type) %>%
  mutate(
    percentage = n / sum(n) * 100,
    label = ifelse(percentage >= 3, paste0(round(percentage, 1), "%"), "")
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    policy_type = factor(policy_type, levels = c("CC", "COMP_E", "COMP_N", "TP", "TPG")),
    loss_ratio_group = factor(
      loss_ratio_group,
      levels = c("No Loss", "Profitable / Acceptable", "Loss-making")
    )
  )

ggplot(profitability_policy,
       aes(x = policy_type, y = percentage, fill = loss_ratio_group)) +
  geom_col(colour = "white", width = 0.8) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = label),
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
    size = 3.2
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(
    title = "Loss Ratio Group by Policy Type",
    subtitle = "Shows profitability composition across different policy types",
    x = "Policy Type",
    y = "Percentage of Policies",
    fill = "Loss Ratio Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "right"
  )
NoteInsights from visuals
  • Most policies have no loss across all policy types, with TP having the highest “No Loss” proportion at 94.7%, followed by TPG at 91.2% and CC at 90.5%.
  • COMP_N looks the riskiest, because it has the highest proportion of Loss-making policies at 20.8%, much higher than the other policy types
  • Profitable / Acceptable policies form a small share overall, but COMP_N has the highest proportion at 8.3%, while COMP_E is next at 4.4%

Statistical Test

Since both policy_type and loss_ratio_group are categorical variables, a Chi-square test of independence was used to validate whether profitability composition differs across policy types.

Show code 
profitability_table <- motor_insurance_final %>%
  filter(!is.na(policy_type), !is.na(loss_ratio_group)) %>%
  count(policy_type, loss_ratio_group) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = loss_ratio_group,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  )

profitability_matrix <- profitability_table %>%
  column_to_rownames("policy_type") %>%
  as.matrix()

chisq.test(profitability_matrix)

    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  profitability_matrix
X-squared = 7921.4, df = 8, p-value < 2.2e-16
NoteStatistical Test Findings
  • The Chi-square test shows a statistically significant association between policy_type and loss_ratio_group (χ² = 7921.4, df = 8, p < 0.001).
  • Most policy types are dominated by the No Loss group, especially TP and TPG, which have very high proportions of no-loss policies.
  • COMP_N stands out as the riskier policy type, as it has a relatively higher proportion of Loss-making policies compared with the other policy types.

2. Underwriting Profit vs Bonus Score

A half-eye plot with embedded boxplot was used to compare underwriting_profit across bonus_score groups. This plot was chosen because it combines the strengths of both a density plot and a boxplot. The half-eye density shows where underwriting profit values are more concentrated, while the boxplot summarises the median and interquartile range. This makes it useful for comparing the shape, spread, and central tendency of profitability across policyholders with different past claims profiles. The red dashed line at zero represents the break-even point.

  • Plot
  • Code
underwriting_bonus_data <- motor_insurance_final %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(bonus_score),
    is.finite(underwriting_profit),
    underwriting_profit >= -1000,
    underwriting_profit <= 1500
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    bonus_score = factor(
      bonus_score,
      levels = c("Good", "Neutral", "Bad")
    )
  )

# Median values for annotation
median_bonus <- underwriting_bonus_data %>%
  group_by(bonus_score) %>%
  summarise(
    median_profit = median(underwriting_profit, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

ggplot(
  underwriting_bonus_data,
  aes(x = underwriting_profit, y = bonus_score, fill = bonus_score)
) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.7,
    width = 0.6,
    justification = -0.2,
    alpha = 0.85,
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.12,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    fill = "white",
    colour = "grey30"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "red",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = median_bonus,
    aes(
      x = median_profit,
      y = bonus_score,
      label = paste0("Median = ", comma(round(median_profit, 0)))
    ),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    nudge_y = 0.28,
    colour = "black",
    size = 3.3,
    hjust = 0
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 80,
    y = 3.35,
    label = "Break-even",
    colour = "red",
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Good" = "#FF6B6B",
      "Neutral" = "#4D96FF",
      "Bad" = "#6BCB3D"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Underwriting Profit by Bonus Score",
    subtitle = "Half-eye plot with boxplot; range limited for readability",
    x = "Underwriting Profit",
    y = "Bonus Score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none"
  )
NoteInsights from visuals
  • Most bonus score groups are concentrated above the break-even line, suggesting that most policies have positive underwriting profit within the displayed range.
  • The Bad bonus score group has the highest median underwriting profit at 342, compared with Neutral = 246 and Good = 236.
  • The Bad group also shows wider variation, but this should be interpreted carefully because it has far fewer policies than the Good group

Statistical Test

Since underwriting_profit is a numerical variable and bonus_score consists of three categorical groups, a Kruskal-Wallis test was used to assess whether underwriting profit differs across bonus score groups. This non-parametric test was selected because underwriting profit is skewed and contains outliers.

Show code 
underwriting_bonus_test <- motor_insurance_final %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(bonus_score),
    is.finite(underwriting_profit)
  )

underwriting_bonus_test %>%
  kruskal_test(underwriting_profit ~ bonus_score)

Since the Kruskal-Wallis test is significant, pairwise Wilcoxon tests were conducted to identify which bonus score groups differ from each other. The Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment was used to control for multiple comparisons.

Show code 
underwriting_bonus_test %>%
  pairwise_wilcox_test(
    underwriting_profit ~ bonus_score,
    p.adjust.method = "BH"
  )

1 underw… Bad    Good     4693 339836    9.92e8 1.47e-181 4.41e-181 ****        
2 underw… Bad    Neutr…   4693   7809    2.10e7 7.44e- 42 1.12e- 41 ****        
3 underw… Good   Neutr… 339836   7809    1.21e9 6.53e- 38 6.53e- 38 ****
NoteStatistical Test Findings
  • The Kruskal-Wallis test shows a statistically significant difference in underwriting_profit across bonus score groups.
  • Pairwise Wilcoxon tests were conducted to identify which specific groups differed.
  • All pairwise comparisons were significant after adjustment: Bad vs Good, Bad vs Neutral, and Good vs Neutral all had p.adj < 0.001.
  • This suggests that bonus_score differs significantly with underwriting profit.

3. Underwriting Profit vs Business Type

A violin plot with boxplot overlay is chosen because underwriting profit is a numerical profitability measure while business type is categorical. Violin shape can tell us where underwriting profit values are concentrated. The boxplot will show us the median and interquartile range.

  • Plot
  • Code
underwriting_business_data <- motor_insurance_final %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(business_type),
    is.finite(underwriting_profit),
    underwriting_profit >= -1000,
    underwriting_profit <= 1500
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    business_type = case_when(
      business_type == "NB" ~ "New Business",
      business_type == "P" ~ "Portfolio",
      business_type == "New Business" ~ "New Business",
      business_type == "Portfolio" ~ "Portfolio",
      TRUE ~ as.character(business_type)
    ),
    business_type = factor(
      business_type,
      levels = c("New Business", "Portfolio")
    )
  )

ggplot(
  underwriting_business_data,
  aes(x = business_type, y = underwriting_profit, fill = business_type)
) +
  geom_violin(
    trim = FALSE,
    alpha = 0.75,
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.12,
    fill = "white",
    colour = "grey30",
    outlier.shape = NA
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "red",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 1.5,
    y = 120,
    label = "Break-even",
    colour = "red",
    size = 3.5
  ) +

    )
  ) +

  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none"
  )
NoteInsights from visuals
  • Both New Business and Portfolio are mostly concentrated above the break-even line: many policies generate positive underwriting profit
  • New Business has more concentration closer to the lower positive profit range, while Portfolio is more concentrated at a slightly higher profit range
  • Both groups still show negative underwriting profit values, meaning some policies are loss-making, but the main concentration is on the profitable side

Statistical Test

A Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used to assess whether underwriting profit differs between New Business and Portfolio policies. This non-parametric test was selected because underwriting_profit is skewed and contains outliers.

Show code 
underwriting_business_test <- motor_insurance_final %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(business_type),
    is.finite(underwriting_profit)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    business_type = case_when(
      business_type == "NB" ~ "New Business",
      business_type == "P" ~ "Portfolio",
      business_type == "New Business" ~ "New Business",
      business_type == "Portfolio" ~ "Portfolio",
      TRUE ~ as.character(business_type)
    ),
    business_type = factor(
      business_type,
      levels = c("New Business", "Portfolio")
    )
  )

wilcox.test(
  underwriting_profit ~ business_type,
  data = underwriting_business_test
)

    Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  underwriting_profit by business_type
W = 9369340678, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0
NoteStatistical Test Findings

  • The Wilcoxon rank-sum test shows a statistically significant difference in underwriting profit between New Business and Portfolio policies.

  • The result is significant with p < 0.001, suggesting that underwriting profit differs across the two business types.

  • This supports the violin plot finding, where Portfolio policies generally appear to have higher underwriting profit than New Business policies.

  • This suggests that existing portfolio policies may be more profitable than newly acquired policies.

4. Driver Age vs Loss Ratio Group

A median-IQR error bar plot was used to compare underwriting profit across driver age bands. The point and line show the median underwriting profit, while the vertical error bars represent the interquartile range, or the middle 50% of policies in each age group.

  • Plot
  • Code
# Prepare data
age_profit_data <- motor_insurance_final %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(driver_age),
    !is.na(underwriting_profit),
    is.finite(driver_age),
    is.finite(underwriting_profit)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    driver_age_band = case_when(
      driver_age < 30 ~ "Below 30",
      driver_age >= 30 & driver_age < 40 ~ "30-39",
      driver_age >= 40 & driver_age < 50 ~ "40-49",
      driver_age >= 50 & driver_age < 60 ~ "50-59",
      driver_age >= 60 ~ "60 and above"
    ),
    driver_age_band = factor(
      driver_age_band,
      levels = c("Below 30", "30-39", "40-49", "50-59", "60 and above")
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(driver_age_band))

# Summarise profitability by age band
age_profit_summary <- age_profit_data %>%
  group_by(driver_age_band) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    median_underwriting_profit = median(underwriting_profit, na.rm = TRUE),
    q1 = quantile(underwriting_profit, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    q3 = quantile(underwriting_profit, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    label = paste0("n = ", scales::comma(n))
  )

# Plot median underwriting profit with IQR
age_profit_summary %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = driver_age_band,
    y = median_underwriting_profit,
    group = 1
  )) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = q1, ymax = q3),
    width = 0.15,
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_line(
    linewidth = 0.9,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    size = 3
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = label),
    position = position_nudge(x = 0.08, y = 8),
    hjust = 0,
    size = 3.3
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Underwriting Profit by Driver Age Band",
    subtitle = "Shows typical profitability and interquartile range across driver age groups",
    x = "Driver Age Band",
    y = "Median Underwriting Profit"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
NoteInsights from Visuals

  • Median underwriting profit is positive across all driver age bands, suggesting that each age group is generally profitable at the median level.

  • The Below 30 group has the highest median underwriting profit, but it also has the smallest sample size compared with the other age bands. Hence, this difference should be interpreted carefully.

  • For the other age bands, median underwriting profit is fairly similar, mostly around the low-to-mid 200 range. This means that driver age does not appear to be a strong standalone factor in explaining underwriting profitability as what we concluded in the correlation plot

Statistical Test

Since underwriting_profit is a numerical variable and driver_age_band consists of five categorical groups, a Kruskal-Wallis test was used to assess whether underwriting profit differs across driver age bands. This non-parametric test was selected because underwriting profit is skewed and contains extreme values.

Show code 
age_profit_test_data <- motor_insurance_final %>%
  filter(
    is.finite(driver_age),
    is.finite(underwriting_profit)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    driver_age_band = case_when(
      driver_age < 30 ~ "Below 30",
      driver_age >= 30 & driver_age < 40 ~ "30-39",
      driver_age >= 40 & driver_age < 50 ~ "40-49",
      driver_age >= 50 & driver_age < 60 ~ "50-59",
      driver_age >= 60 ~ "60 and above"
    ),
    driver_age_band = factor(
      driver_age_band,
      levels = c("Below 30", "30-39", "40-49", "50-59", "60 and above")
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(driver_age_band))

age_profit_test_data %>%
  kruskal_test(underwriting_profit ~ driver_age_band)

  • The Kruskal-Wallis test shows a statistically significant difference in underwriting profit across driver age bands (χ² = 961.54, df = 4, p < 0.001). This suggests that underwriting profit is not distributed exactly the same across all age groups.

5. Average Loss Ratio vs Year

  • Plot

yearly_loss_ratio <- motor_insurance_final %>%
  filter(is.finite(loss_ratio)) %>%
  mutate(year_num = as.numeric(as.character(year))) %>%
  group_by(year_num) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_loss_ratio = mean(loss_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

p_temporal_loss <- ggplot(
  yearly_loss_ratio,
  aes(x = year_num, y = avg_loss_ratio)
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 1,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "red",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_line(
    colour = "mediumpurple",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    colour = "mediumpurple",
    size = 3
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = round(avg_loss_ratio, 2)),
    vjust = -0.8,
    size = 4,
    colour = "mediumpurple4"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = max(yearly_loss_ratio$year_num),
    y = 1.02,
    label = "Break-even",
    colour = "red",
    hjust = 1,
    size = 4
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = yearly_loss_ratio$year_num
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0.6, 1.05),
    labels = label_number(accuracy = 0.01)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Temporal Trend of Average Loss Ratio",
    subtitle = "Average loss ratio by year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Loss Ratio"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  transition_reveal(year_num)

animate(
  p_temporal_loss,
  nframes = 80,
  fps = 10,
  width = 800,
  height = 500,
  end_pause = 20,
  renderer = gifski_renderer()
)
NoteInsights from Visuals

  • The average loss ratio increased from 0.67 in 2022 to 0.73 in 2023, and further to 0.87 in 2024.

  • Although the average loss ratio remains below the break-even point of 1.00 across all three years, the upward trend suggests that portfolio profitability is weakening over time.

  • This means that a larger share of premium collected is being used to cover incurred claims each year.

  • If this trend continues, the portfolio may face greater profitability pressure, as the average loss ratio is moving closer to the loss-making threshold.

Statistical Test

Since loss_ratio is a numerical variable and year consists of three groups, a Kruskal-Wallis test was used to assess whether loss ratio differs across years. This non-parametric test was selected because loss ratio is highly skewed and contains extreme values.

2. Claim Frequency vs Vehicle Value Band

# Prepare data
vehicle_claim_freq_heatmap_data <- motor_insurance_final %>%
  mutate(
    claim_frequency_group = case_when(
      claim_frequency == 0 ~ "No Claim",
      claim_frequency > 0 & claim_frequency <= 1 ~ "Low Claim Frequency",
      claim_frequency > 1 ~ "High Claim Frequency"
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(vehicle_value),
    !is.na(claim_frequency_group),
    is.finite(vehicle_value),

  count(vehicle_value_band, claim_frequency_group) %>%
  group_by(vehicle_value_band) %>%
  mutate(
    percentage = n / sum(n),
    label = paste0(scales::comma(n), "\n", scales::percent(percentage, accuracy = 0.1))
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

  scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = c("#d73027", "#fee08b", "#1a9850"),
    labels = scales::percent
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Claim Frequency Group by Vehicle Value Band",
    subtitle = "Heatmap showing claim frequency composition within each vehicle value band",
    x = "Vehicle Value Band",
    y = "Claim Frequency Group",
    fill = "Percentage of Policies"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
NoteInsights from Visuals

  • Across all vehicle value bands, the majority of policies fall under the No Claim group. However, this proportion gradually declines as vehicle value increases, from 88.8% in the Low band to 82.4% in the High band.

  • The proportion of High Claim Frequency policies increases steadily across vehicle value bands, rising from 7.3% in the Low band to 11.5% in the High band. This suggests that higher-value vehicles are associated with a greater concentration of more frequent claims.

  • A similar upward pattern is seen for Low Claim Frequency policies, which increase from 3.9% to 6.1% across the bands. Overall, this indicates that higher vehicle value bands tend to have slightly less stable claim experience compared with lower-value bands.

Statistical Test

Since both vehicle_value_band and claim_frequency_group are categorical variables, a Chi-square test of independence was used to assess whether claim frequency composition differs across vehicle value bands.

Show code 
vehicle_claim_freq_test_data <- motor_insurance_final %>%
  mutate(
    claim_frequency_group = case_when(
      claim_frequency == 0 ~ "No Claim",
      claim_frequency > 0 & claim_frequency <= 1 ~ "Low Claim Frequency",
      claim_frequency > 1 ~ "High Claim Frequency"
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(
    is.finite(vehicle_value),
    vehicle_value > 0,
    !is.na(claim_frequency_group)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    vehicle_value_band = ntile(vehicle_value, 4),
    vehicle_value_band = factor(
      vehicle_value_band,
      levels = 1:4,
      labels = c("Low", "Lower-Mid", "Upper-Mid", "High")
    ),
    claim_frequency_group = factor(
      claim_frequency_group,
      levels = c("No Claim", "Low Claim Frequency", "High Claim Frequency")
    )
  )

vehicle_claim_freq_table <- vehicle_claim_freq_test_data %>%
  count(vehicle_value_band, claim_frequency_group) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = claim_frequency_group,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  )

vehicle_claim_freq_matrix <- vehicle_claim_freq_table %>%
  column_to_rownames("vehicle_value_band") %>%
  as.matrix()

chisq.test(vehicle_claim_freq_matrix)

    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  vehicle_claim_freq_matrix
X-squared = 1577.9, df = 6, p-value < 2.2e-16
NoteStatistical Test Findings

  • The Chi-square test shows a statistically significant association between vehicle_value_band and claim_frequency_group (χ² = 1577.9, df = 6, p < 0.001). Claim frequency group is not the same across vehicle value bands.

  • This supports the heatmap, where the proportion of No Claim policies decreases as vehicle value increases, while both Low Claim Frequency and High Claim Frequency policies increase.

  • Higher-value vehicles seem to have slightly more claim activity compared with lower-value vehicles. However, most policies still have no claims across all vehicle value bands, so vehicle value is related to claim frequency, but it is not the only factor explaining claims.

Statistical Test

Since both claim_frequency_group and circulation_area are categorical variables, a Chi-square test of independence was used to assess whether claim frequency composition differs between Urban and Rural policies.

Show code 
circulation_claim_freq_test_data <- motor_insurance_final %>%
  mutate(
    claim_frequency_group = case_when(
      claim_frequency == 0 ~ "No Claim",
      claim_frequency > 0 & claim_frequency <= 1 ~ "Low Claim Frequency",
      claim_frequency > 1 ~ "High Claim Frequency",
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(circulation_area),
    !is.na(claim_frequency_group)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    claim_frequency_group = factor(
      claim_frequency_group,
      levels = c("No Claim", "Low Claim Frequency", "High Claim Frequency")
    )
  )

circulation_claim_freq_table <- circulation_claim_freq_test_data %>%
  count(circulation_area, claim_frequency_group) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = claim_frequency_group,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  )

circulation_claim_freq_matrix <- circulation_claim_freq_table %>%
  column_to_rownames("circulation_area") %>%
  as.matrix()

chisq.test(circulation_claim_freq_matrix)

    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  circulation_claim_freq_matrix
X-squared = 233.44, df = 2, p-value < 2.2e-16
NoteStatistical Test Findings

  • The Chi-square test shows a statistically significant association between circulation_area and claim_frequency_group (χ² = 233.44, df = 2, p < 0.001). This suggests that claim frequency group is not distributed exactly the same between Urban and Rural policies.

  • This supports the visual analysis, where Urban policies have a slightly higher proportion of High Claim Frequency policies, while Rural policies have a slightly higher proportion of No Claim policies.

  • Urban policies appear to have slightly more claim activity than Rural policies. However, most policies in both groups still fall under the No Claim group, so the difference is statistically significant but not very large visually.

4. Claim Severity vs Driving Experience Group

  • Plot
  • Code
# Prepare data: only policies with claims
severity_exp_ridge <- motor_insurance_final %>%
  filter(
    total_claims > 0,
    is.finite(driving_experience),
    is.finite(claim_severity),
    driving_experience >= 0,
    driving_experience <= 70,
    claim_severity >= 0,
    claim_severity <= 5000
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    driving_experience_group = cut(
      driving_experience,
      breaks = seq(0, 70, by = 10),
      include.lowest = TRUE,
      right = FALSE
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(driving_experience_group))

# Ridgeline density plot
ggplot(
  severity_exp_ridge,
  aes(
    x = claim_severity,
    y = driving_experience_group,
    fill = driving_experience_group
  )
) +
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 1.4,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    colour = "white",
    linewidth = 0.35,
    alpha = 0.85
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::comma,
    breaks = seq(0, 5000, by = 1000)
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(
    title = "Claim Severity Distribution by Driving Experience Group",
    subtitle = "Only policies with claims are included; claim severity is capped at 5,000 for readability",
    x = "Claim Severity",
    y = "Driving Experience Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none"
  )

# Spearman correlation test using original continuous variables
severity_exp_test <- motor_insurance_final %>%
  filter(
    total_claims > 0,
    is.finite(driving_experience),
    is.finite(claim_severity)
  )

severity_exp_test %>%
  cor_test(
    driving_experience,
    claim_severity,
    method = "spearman"
  )
NoteInsights from Visuals

  • Claim severity is right-skewed across all driving experience groups, with most claims concentrated at the lower severity range.

  • The distribution shapes are broadly similar across experience groups, suggesting that driving experience may not be a strong standalone factor in explaining claim severity.

  • Some groups, especially the 30–40 and 50–60 experience groups, show longer right tails, indicating occasional high-severity claims.

  • Since the visual differences are not very strong, a Spearman correlation test should be used to statistically validate whether driving experience is associated with claim severity.

Statistical Test

Since claim_severity is a numerical variable and driving_experience_group consists of several categorical groups, a Kruskal-Wallis test was used to assess whether claim severity differs across driving experience groups. This non-parametric test was selected because claim severity is highly skewed and contains high-severity outliers.

Show code 
severity_exp_ridge %>%
  kruskal_test(claim_severity ~ driving_experience_group)
# A tibble: 1 × 6
  .y.                n statistic    df        p method        
* <chr>          <int>     <dbl> <int>    <dbl> <chr>         
1 claim_severity 49685      96.7     6 1.23e-18 Kruskal-Wallis
NoteStatistical Test Findings

  • The Kruskal-Wallis test shows a statistically significant difference in claim_severity across driving experience groups. The result is significant with H(6) = 96.68, p < 0.001.

  • At least one driving experience group has a different claim severity distribution.

  • Since the ridgeline plot shows broadly similar shapes across groups, the difference appears statistically significant but not very visually large. This may be influenced by the large number of claim records used in the test.

Summary and Recommendations

Summary

This study applied visual analytics and statistical validation to explore profitability and volatility in a Spanish motor insurance portfolio. Overall, the portfolio remains profitable, with average loss ratio below the break-even point of 1.00. However, profitability is weakening over time, as average loss ratio increased from 0.67 in 2022 to 0.87 in 2024. Claim volatility is mainly driven by claim severity, where most claims are low-cost but a small number of high-severity claims pull the mean upward.

Key Findings

  • Policy type is strongly associated with profitability. COMP_N has the highest loss-making share at 20.8%, while TP and TPG perform well with 94.7% and 91.2% no-loss policies respectively. The Chi-square test confirms a significant association between policy_type and loss_ratio_group (χ² = 7921.4, p < 0.001).

  • Profitability weakened over time. Average loss ratio increased from 0.67 in 2022 to 0.87 in 2024. Kruskal-Wallis and pairwise Wilcoxon tests show that loss ratio differs significantly across all year pairs (p < 0.001).

  • Business type matters. Portfolio policies show higher underwriting profit than New Business policies, and the Wilcoxon test confirms a significant difference (p < 0.001). This suggests that existing policies may be more profitable than newly acquired ones.

  • Bonus score shows a counterintuitive pattern. Underwriting profit differs significantly across bonus score groups (H(2) = 977.21, p < 0.001). The Bad group has the highest median underwriting profit, but this should be interpreted carefully because it is a small group.

  • Claim severity is the main volatility concern. Claim severity is strongly right-skewed, with median severity around 498 and mean severity around 849. This suggests that a small number of expensive claims may contribute disproportionately to volatility.

  • Continuous variables are weaker predictors. Driver age, vehicle age, driving experience, and vehicle value show weak relationships with key outcomes, suggesting that categorical segmentation gives clearer insights than continuous variables alone.

Recommendations for Future Research

  • Investigate the increase in loss ratio from 2022 to 2024 to determine whether it is caused by claim inflation, pricing gaps, portfolio mix changes, or external factors.

  • Review COMP_N policies to understand whether the higher loss-making share is due to pricing, claim severity, coverage structure, or customer risk profile.

  • Study the strong performance of TP and TPG policies to assess whether these segments can be grown sustainably.

  • Investigate the Bad bonus score anomaly to determine whether the higher median profit is due to pricing strategy, coverage mix, or small-group effects.

  • Include external variables such as repair cost trends, inflation, accident rates, weather, and traffic conditions to better explain profitability and volatility patterns.

  • Use more granular claim-level data, such as claim type, cause of accident, repair category, and settlement status, to better understand high-severity claims.

Overall Conclusion

Overall, profitability and volatility in this portfolio are not driven by one single factor. Policy type, business type, bonus score, and year show significant relationships with profitability, while claim severity remains the key source of volatility. Although the portfolio is still profitable, the rising loss ratio suggests emerging profitability pressure that should be monitored and investigated further.
